# FDG5115

> DO NOT pass value types by read-only reference (`in`).

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 5.8.3 Parameter Passing.

## How it is checked

- Check: fdg (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: FDG5115
- Automatic fix: not applied automatically (the fix can break callers)
- Severity: library warning, application none, test none
- Status: draft

Message: Do not pass the value type parameter '{0}' of '{1}' by read-only reference

Library only: the text and the Barton annotation are about public and protected members, which cannot change the modifier later without breaking callers; in private or internal code the in modifier can be useful. FDG5115 reports an in or ref readonly parameter of a value type (a struct, an enum, or a type parameter constrained to a value type) of an externally visible method, constructor, delegate, operator or indexer. Overrides and interface implementations are not reported, and neither is an in parameter of an unconstrained type parameter. Changing the modifier changes the public API, so the fix is breaking; there is no code fix.

## From the book

The main benefit of passing a value type by read-only reference is to reduce the cost of copying the value when the type is large. Since the guidance for value types is that they should be small (section 4.2), the performance benefit is slight. Conversely, if your method reads a property or invokes a method—without the appropriate `readonly` modifier—on an `in` parameter, you end up paying the cost silently. Once the compiler has made two defensive copies (or one copy if the type is small), your API now pays a performance penalty for the modifier, rather than receiving a performance boost.

This performance penalty risk, combined with some CLR languages having unpleasant syntax for passing by reference, means you should rarely, if ever, use the `in` modifier in public or protected methods.

> **Jeremy Barton:** The `in` modifier, like large structs, can be useful in private or internal code. The edge cases and gotchas to this modifier can be noticed in private code and changed to pass-by-value or “full” `ref`. Since public (and protected) members can’t freely change from `in` to `ref`—or from `in` to by-value—when performance testing says to do so, we advise against using the `in` modifier in those members.
